contentSections.heading: Quick answer
paragraphs: Choose OpenClaw if you want many messaging channels and native apps for phone and computer, and Hermes Agent if you want an agent that learns from use. The software is free for both, and Hostinger's managed plan serves either. What matters is what the agent will do; see the profiles below.

contentSections.heading: What each one is
paragraphs: Both are open-source AI assistants under the MIT license that you install and talk to through Telegram, WhatsApp or another messaging app. The license costs nothing; what sets them apart is the interface, the memory and who maintains the project.

**OpenClaw** is maintained by the OpenClaw Foundation, a non-profit organization. The official README says state, memory and credentials stay on the device where it runs, with no paid plan, hosted service or token. It has a web interface (Control UI), a command line and native apps for macOS, iOS, Android, Windows and Linux. On Hostinger it is available managed or on a VPS, as the [OpenClaw managed or VPS guide](/en/reviews/openclaw-hostinger-managed-or-vps) shows.

**Hermes Agent** is made by Nous Research, a company that develops AI models. Its signature is the learning loop: the agent organizes its own memory between sessions, creates and improves its own skills, searches past conversations and builds a model of the user with Honcho. It has a full terminal and Hermes Desktop, a desktop app with an installer for Windows and macOS. The project page does not state a price for the software. It mentions Nous Portal, a subscription with tools such as web search, browsing and image generation, with no price given. Nous Portal is one way to pay for the model, not the only one.

contentSections.heading: What it really costs
paragraphs: The software costs nothing in either case. The real spending comes from three places:
bullets: **Server.** It can be your own computer, switched on all the time, or a VPS, a rented virtual server. A VPS gives you root access, full control of the machine, but you are the one who updates and secures the system. The more RAM, the more programs run at once without stalling.
**Managed plan.** Hostinger installs, updates and maintains the assistant. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are on the same plan, “AI automation apps”.

**AI model.** The assistant asks a model, such as Claude, GPT or Gemini, for its replies, and the model charges for use. There are two ways to pay: your own API key, where the provider bills you directly, or AI credits bought from Hostinger. The managed OpenClaw and Hermes Agent plans come with starting credit; top-ups do not appear on a public page, so check the dashboard. For Nous Portal, the price is not stated on the project page.
postParagraphs: The monthly cost of model use is not stated in the sources: it depends on the model you pick and the number of conversations. That is why this guide gives no estimate of a monthly total.

contentSections.heading: Before you install
paragraphs: Before you start, confirm three things. They apply to both agents.
bullets: **AI model.** The agent does not answer on its own: it asks a model from another company for its replies. On Hostinger, you use the plan's AI credits or your own API key, which the program uses to talk to the provider. The provider charges for use, directly to you.

**A messaging channel.** Telegram is the simplest route. You create the bot in BotFather, Telegram's official bot for making bots, and keep the token. WhatsApp joins as a linked device, by scanning a QR code.

**Who looks after the server.** On the managed plan, Hostinger handles updates and security. On a VPS, updating is up to you, with the Update button in Docker Manager, and so is the server's security. Docker is the program that runs each application isolated in a container.
postParagraphs: If you install OpenClaw yourself, with npm, it requires Node.js 24.16 or newer, or 26.1 or newer. The project's security policy does not support versions 22, 23 and 25.

contentSections.heading: Each project's security
paragraphs: The two projects' security policies say who the agent was built for. Read them before deciding how to expose it.
bullets: **OpenClaw** (SECURITY.md in the openclaw/openclaw repository): built for one trusted operator, not for several people who do not know each other. Whoever can talk to the agent can make it use its tools. For more than one person, the project recommends one server per person. Do not expose the gateway directly to the public internet. Plugins run in the same process and are treated as trusted code, so install only what you know.

**Hermes Agent** (SECURITY.md in the NousResearch/hermes-agent repository): built for a single person. Do not expose the gateway to the internet without a VPN, Tailscale or a firewall. Run the agent as a user without root privileges and review third-party skills and plugins by reading the code, not just the SKILL.md file.
postParagraphs: For the choice between managed and VPS, the question is who looks after the data and the credentials. The guide to [managed or VPS for OpenClaw](/en/reviews/openclaw-hostinger-managed-or-vps) covers this in detail.

contentSections.heading: Who each one suits
paragraphs: Both are open source and charge no license fee. The choice depends on what you want the agent to do, not on the software.

image.alt: Board with four profiles and the answer for each: many channels and a phone app lead to OpenClaw; an agent that learns and creates its own skills leads to Hermes Agent; not wanting to look after a server leads to the managed plan; wanting root and other programs leads to a VPS
image.caption: According to each project's documentation.

bullets: **You want many channels and a phone app:** OpenClaw. The README mentions more than 20 channels and ships native apps for phone and computer, besides the web Control UI.
**You want an agent that learns from use:** Hermes Agent. It organizes its own memory, creates and improves its own skills and searches past conversations.
**You want root access and other programs on the same server, such as a website or n8n:** a VPS, with either one. Root is administrator access, with full control of the server.
**You don't want to install or look after a server:** the managed plan, with either one. Hostinger installs and updates.
postParagraphs: Nobody on the team uses either of them. The profiles come from the projects' documentation, not from our experience.

contentSections.heading: Frequently asked questions
bullets: Are OpenClaw and Hermes Agent free? Both programs are open source, under the MIT license, and you do not pay for the software. You pay for the server or the managed plan and for AI model use. Hermes also has a Nous Portal subscription, but its price does not appear in the project's documentation.
Does it work with Telegram? Yes, with both. You create the bot in BotFather and paste the token into the configuration.

Do you need to know how to code? To set up the managed plan, no: you choose the channels and paste the token. On a VPS, you need the basics of servers, such as root, Docker and updates. Coding only comes in if you want to change the project's code.

Is it safe? It depends on how you use it. Both security policies ask for the same care: use by one trusted person, no direct exposure to the internet, and a review of whatever you install from third parties.

Which one should I choose if I already use Claude Code? Claude Code is a tool for coding in the terminal and does not replace either of them. Both accept an Anthropic key: OpenClaw lists Anthropic among its providers, and the Hermes Agent README lists the Anthropic key among its secrets. If you want an agent that learns from use, Hermes Agent fits better. If you want many channels and a phone app, OpenClaw.
